lesson.menu_title: The Client Is a Doctor -- Prescribers, Advocacy and Access
lesson.menu_desc: The doctors who prescribe, the ones other doctors follow, and the language of the visit report -- 38 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 4 -- The Client Is a Doctor
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Renato Annunciato | Lesson 4 -- The Client Is a Doctor

listenings.text: I see representatives from the industry almost every week, and I can tell you in one minute whether I will see that person again. It has almost nothing to do with the product. The ones I trust are the ones who know what I actually treat. If somebody comes into my clinic and talks about an indication I have never worked with, I know they did not read anything about me before they came. The second thing is time. I have twenty minutes between consultations, and a representative who needs fifteen of them to arrive at the point is a representative I will not book again. Tell me what is new, tell me what changed since last time, and tell me what you want from me. The last one is the one nobody says out loud, and it is the one I respect most. And please do not ask me to endorse something in front of my residents before you have shown me the data. My credibility with them is the only thing in this room that is really mine.

For my first three years in this industry I treated every visit as a sale, and I was wrong in a way that took me a long time to see. I would prepare the message, deliver the message, and leave with a commitment that I wrote down and reported. The numbers looked fine. What I did not notice was that the doctors who mattered most had stopped telling me anything. They answered my questions and nothing else. A colleague who had been doing this for twenty years gave me one instruction. Go into the next four visits with no message at all, and come out with three things you did not know. It felt like wasting four visits. Two of them turned into the strongest advocacy I have ever had, because for the first time I understood what those doctors were actually trying to solve. A visit where you learn nothing is not a short visit. It is a visit you will have to repeat.

reading.rtitle: Visit Report -- Key Opinion Leader, Sao Paulo
paras: Doctor Mariana Prado, who runs a private practice in the west of Sao Paulo, is the strongest prescriber in the territory. She is a neurologist whose consultations are booked eight weeks ahead, and the waiting list for the procedure we support is the longest in the region. She is also the doctor other specialists call when they are not sure, which is what makes her a key opinion leader and not simply a large account.

The visit had one purpose: to understand why her advocacy has cooled since March. The protocol that we presented at the congress last year is still the one she follows, and she endorsed it publicly at the time. What changed is not the science. She explained that two of the indications she treats most often are now covered by a competitor programme that pays for the first consultation, which means her patients arrive already committed to another brand.

She asked for two things. The first is a written summary of the new safety data, which she wants in a form she can show to the residents she trains. The second is a referral pathway: she sends patients to three colleagues in the east of the city, and she wants those clinics included in the same support programme. Neither request costs us anything we do not already have.

We committed to two actions. Medical Affairs will send the summary within ten working days, and I will map the three clinics she referred to and confirm whether they qualify. Her credibility with the younger specialists is worth more to us than any single account, and losing it quietly would be the most expensive thing that could happen in this territory this year.
